title: Plant parts we eat, and how a cactus, a lotus and a banyan use theirs

summary.text: Put a piece of brinjal and a piece of potato in a bowl of water. The brinjal floats and the potato sinks. Every vegetable is a part of a plant: a root, a stem, a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a seed. What is inside each part shows the job it did for the plant. In this unit you sort the food in your kitchen by plant part, and test which parts float. You also meet three plants with very different parts: a cactus in a dry desert, a lotus in a pond and a huge banyan tree.
summary.art: A steel bowl of water with a piece of brinjal and a palak leaf floating on top, and a piece of potato and some chana lying on the bottom.

intro.hook: Next time someone washes vegetables, watch the bowl. Some pieces float on top. Some pieces go to the bottom. Which ones float in your home?
intro.text: Every vegetable we eat is one part of a plant. A carrot is a root. Palak is a leaf. A brinjal is a fruit, and chana is a seed. These parts are not all made the same way inside. Some are packed tight with food. Some have tiny spaces full of air. Before you read on, make a guess. Will a piece of potato float or sink? You are going to find out.
intro.art: A child at a kitchen sink looking closely into a bowl of water where some vegetable pieces float and some lie at the bottom.

outcomes: By the end I can say which part of a plant a food is: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit or seed.
By the end I can test which plant parts float and which sink, and say what my test showed.
By the end I can say why some plant parts sink (packed with stored food) and some float (tiny air spaces inside).
By the end I can compare the roots, stems and leaves of a cactus, a lotus and a banyan.
By the end I can say how each of those plants' parts helps them live where they grow.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what I saw.

terms.meaning: One piece of a plant. Each piece has its own job: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit or seed.
terms.example: A carrot is the root of the carrot plant. Palak is the leaf of the palak plant.
terms.art: A carrot plant pulled up, with their orange root and their feathery green leaves.

terms.meaning: Safe to eat. Only some plant parts are edible.
terms.example: The leaf of a drumstick tree is edible. We cook it as murungai keerai.
terms.art: A bunch of small drumstick leaves on a plate next to a drumstick.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. To a scientist, a tomato is a fruit.
terms.example: Cut a tomato, a brinjal or a cucumber. You find seeds inside, so each one is a fruit.
terms.art: A tomato, a brinjal and a cucumber cut in half, showing their seeds.

terms.meaning: Food a plant has made and kept inside a part, to use later.
terms.example: A potato, a carrot and a chana seed are packed with stored food.
terms.art: A potato, a carrot and a few chana with a small picture of a lunch box beside them.

terms.meaning: A tiny gap inside a plant part that is filled with air.
terms.example: A leaf has many air spaces inside. That is one reason a leaf floats.
terms.art: A palak leaf floating on water, with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny gaps between its cells.

terms.meaning: A thing floats if it stays on top of the water. It sinks if it goes down to the bottom.
terms.example: A piece of brinjal floats. A piece of potato sinks.
terms.art: A glass of water with a brinjal piece at the top and a potato piece at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A hard, sharp point. On a cactus, the spines are leaves that have changed shape.
terms.example: A cactus has spines instead of flat green leaves.
terms.art: A close-up of a round cactus covered in clusters of sharp spines.

terms.meaning: A root that grows down from a branch into the soil and holds the branch up, like a pillar.
terms.example: A banyan tree has many prop roots hanging from her branches.
terms.art: A banyan tree with thick roots growing from the branches straight down into the ground.

explanations.concept: Every food from a plant is one of the plant's parts
explanations.context: This card explains how to tell which part of a plant you are eating.
explanations.definition: The plant foods we eat are roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits or seeds. Each part had its own job for the plant.
explanations.description: A carrot and a radish are roots. They grew down into the soil and stored food. Sugarcane and lotus stem are stems. Palak, cabbage and curry leaves are leaves. Cauliflower and banana flower are flowers. A cook calls tomato, brinjal and bhindi vegetables. But they grew from flowers and hold seeds, so to a scientist they are fruits. Rice, wheat, dal and peanuts are seeds.
examples: Leaf: palak, cabbage, curry leaves, drumstick leaves.
Fruit: tomato, brinjal, bhindi, cucumber, drumstick, mango.
Seed: rice, wheat, toor dal, chana, peanuts.
explanations.art: A thali with six small heaps: a carrot, a piece of sugarcane, palak leaves, a cauliflower floret, a tomato and some rice, each with a label for its plant part.

explanations.concept: Why some plant parts float and others sink
explanations.context: This card explains the float test, where some vegetable pieces floated and some sank.
explanations.definition: A plant part that is packed tight with stored food sinks in water. A plant part with many tiny air spaces floats.
explanations.description: A potato, a carrot and a dry chana seed are packed with food that the plant saved for later. There is little room inside for air, so they sink. A brinjal is soft and spongy inside, with many tiny air spaces. A leaf has air spaces too, because a leaf takes in air to make food. The air helps them float. Cutting a potato into a tiny piece does not help. The tiny piece sinks too, because what is inside is the same.
examples: Potato piece: sinks. It is packed with stored food.
Dry chana: sinks. A seed is packed with food for the baby plant inside.
Brinjal piece: floats. It is spongy, with air spaces.
Palak leaf: floats. It has air spaces inside.
explanations.art: Two zoomed-in circles: one showing a potato packed tight with tiny grains of food, one showing a brinjal with many small air gaps.

explanations.concept: A cactus, a lotus and a banyan: same parts, different homes
explanations.context: This card compares three plants that live in very different places.
explanations.definition: Every plant has roots, a stem and leaves, but their shapes are very different. Each plant's parts suit the place where the plant lives.
explanations.description: A cactus lives where it hardly rains. Their thick green stem stores water and makes food, and their spines are leaves that lose almost no water. A lotus lives in a pond, with their stem in the mud where there is little air. Long tunnels of air run down the leaf stalks to the stem. A banyan is a huge tree. Roots grow down from her branches into the soil and hold the branches up like pillars.
examples: Cactus: a fat, green stem that stores water, and spines instead of flat leaves.
Lotus: a stem in the mud, long stalks with air tunnels, and big leaves on the water.
Banyan: prop roots that hang from the branches and become new trunks.
explanations.art: Three panels side by side: a cactus in dry sand, a lotus in a pond with her stalks going down into the mud, and a banyan tree with roots hanging from her branches.

explanations.concept: Does a plant feel what each part is doing?
explanations.context: This card is about whether a plant senses and decides with all their parts.
explanations.description: Plants feel and decide with every part. A banyan's hanging root senses which way is down and keeps growing towards the ground. A root senses wet soil and grows that way. A leaf senses light. The parts send signals to each other, so the whole plant acts together. Some scientists describe this as automatic responses, and do not use words like feel or decide.
examples: A banyan's hanging roots grow straight down towards the soil.
A cactus's roots grow fast just after rain, while the soil is wet.
A money plant's stem bends towards the window.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants behave
perspectives.explanation: A plant senses gravity, water, light and touch with every part, and decides how to grow. Each part sends signals to the others.
These are automatic responses to gravity, water and light. They call them 'responses' and do not use the words 'feel' or 'decide'.

explanations.art: A banyan branch with a thin new root hanging down, and a small arrow showing it growing towards the soil below.

agreed.text: All the plant food we eat comes from six kinds of plant part: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
agreed.evidence: Cut and look: a carrot grows in the soil like a root, a tomato has seeds inside like every fruit, and a dal grain sprouts like a seed.

agreed.text: Plant parts packed with stored food usually sink in water. Parts with many air spaces float.
agreed.evidence: In the float test, a potato piece and dry chana sank. A brinjal piece and a palak leaf floated.

agreed.text: A cactus stores water in a thick stem, and their spines are changed leaves.
agreed.evidence: Cut a cactus stem and it is wet and green inside. Spines grow from the stem where leaves would grow on other plants.

agreed.text: A lotus has air tunnels in their stalks and underground stem.
agreed.evidence: Cut a lotus stem across and you see a ring of holes. Air travels through these tunnels to the parts in the mud.

challenging.claim: Heavy things sink and light things float.
challenging.for: A big stone sinks and a tiny feather floats, so weight seems to decide.
challenging.against: A big piece of brinjal floats and a tiny crumb of potato sinks. What matters is what is inside, not how big or heavy the piece is.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make before the float test.

challenging.claim: A tomato is a vegetable, not a fruit.
challenging.for: We cook tomatoes in rasam and sambar, not in sweets. In the kitchen, a tomato is used like a vegetable.
challenging.against: A tomato grows from a flower and has seeds inside. So to a scientist, a tomato is a fruit. Both words are right in their own place.
challenging.context: This card is about two ways of naming the same food.

challenging.claim: Cactus plants come from the deserts of India.
challenging.for: Prickly pear cactus grows wild on dry roadsides in many parts of India.
challenging.against: Almost all cactus plants first grew in North and South America. People brought prickly pear to India. The thorny plants of the Thar, like khejri, are not cactus plants.
challenging.context: This card is about where cactus plants come from.

big_questions.q: Why does a potato keep so much food inside, when the plant could use that food straight away?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the plant needs when a new shoot starts to grow.

big_questions.q: A lotus lives in water but needs air. How does air reach the parts in the mud?
big_questions.hint: Remember the holes in a slice of lotus stem.

big_questions.q: When you eat a carrot, you eat what the plant saved for later. Whose food is it really?
big_questions.hint: Think about who made the food, and who it was saved for.

big_questions.q: A cactus, a lotus and a banyan look nothing alike. Why do they all have roots, a stem and leaves?
big_questions.hint: Think about the jobs every plant must do, wherever they live.

how_we_found_out.story: Water lilies and lotus plants grow their stems in pond mud. Mud has almost no air in it, but the stems need air to stay alive. For a long time, scientists thought air reached them only by creeping slowly down the leaf stalks. In 1980, a scientist named John Dacey studied the yellow water lily. He found that air does not just creep. Young leaves, warmed by the sun, push air down the stalks. The air flows through the stem in the mud, and comes back up and out through older leaves. Dacey called it an internal wind. In 1988, two scientists in Germany, Mevi-Schütz and Wolfgang Grosse, found a flow of air through the lotus too, driven by the warmth of the sun on the leaves. Scientists are still studying exactly how the lotus pushes the air.
how_we_found_out.who: John Dacey; Mevi-Schütz and Wolfgang Grosse in Germany
how_we_found_out.when: 1980 for the water lily; 1988 for the lotus
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That air reaches the stems of pond plants only by creeping slowly down the stalks. Dacey showed that warm young leaves push air down, so it flows through the plant like a wind.
how_we_found_out.art: A cut-away drawing of a pond: lotus leaves on top in the sun, arrows showing air going down one stalk, through the stem in the mud, and up another stalk.

story.title: The Brinjal That Would Not Sink
story.note: Thamarai thandu is the Tamil name for lotus stem. The Thimmamma Marrimanu banyan is in Andhra Pradesh and is one of the largest trees in the world by the area under her branches. Kavya, Paati and Arjun are made up.
text: Kavya was seven, and she lived in Madurai with her grandmother. Everyone called her grandmother Paati. On Sunday mornings, Kavya helped Paati wash the vegetables for sambar.
This Sunday her cousin Arjun had come from Bengaluru. He was six. He stood on a stool at the sink, watching.

Paati filled a big steel bowl with water. Kavya dropped in the pieces of brinjal. They bobbed up and floated on top. Then she dropped in the pieces of potato. Plop, plop. They went straight to the bottom.
"The potato is heavy, so it sinks," said Arjun. "The brinjal is light, so it floats."
Kavya looked at the bowl. The biggest piece of brinjal was bigger than any piece of potato. "Let's test it," she said.

She picked out the biggest brinjal piece and pushed it down to the bottom. When she let go, it shot back up. Then she broke off a tiny crumb of potato, as small as a grain of rice. She dropped it in. It sank, slowly, all the way down.
Arjun stared. "But it's so small!"
"So it isn't about big or small," said Kavya. "It's about what is inside."

Paati smiled and cut a brinjal piece open. "Look closely," she said. Inside, the brinjal was soft and spongy, like a bath sponge. "There are tiny spaces full of air in there," Paati said. Then she cut a potato. Inside it was firm and wet and white. "A potato is packed with food the plant stored for later. There is no room for much air."
Kavya put a palak leaf on the water. It floated too. "Does a leaf have air inside?" she asked.
"Yes," said Paati. "A leaf takes in air to make the plant's food. So a leaf is full of tiny air spaces."

Next Paati took out something Arjun had never seen. It was a long, pale stick, like a thin cucumber. "This is thamarai thandu," she said. "Lotus stem." She cut a slice and held it up to the window. The slice was full of holes, in a ring like a flower.
"Why does it have holes?" asked Arjun.
Kavya thought about it. "Lotus plants grow in ponds," she said slowly. "This stem was down in the mud. Maybe the holes are for air."

"You are right," said Paati. "Mud has almost no air. These tunnels carry air down from the leaves on top of the pond. When I was a girl near Thanjavur, our temple tank was full of lotus. We children used to break a leaf stalk and look at the holes inside."
Arjun laughed. "A plant with straws inside!"
Then Arjun remembered something. "In my school there is a cactus in a pot," he said. "It has no leaves at all. Only prickles."

"The prickles are the leaves," said Kavya. She had read it in a book. "A cactus lives where it hardly rains. Thin, flat leaves would dry out. So the cactus has spines, and keeps water in a fat green stem."
"And the big tree near Kavya's school?" asked Paati. "The one with roots hanging down like ropes?"
"The banyan!" said Kavya. "Her roots grow down from the branches. When they reach the ground, they get thick, like pillars."

"In Andhra Pradesh there is a banyan called Thimmamma Marrimanu," said Paati. "She has so many pillar roots that she covers more ground than two football fields. People walk inside her like walking in a forest. And it is all one tree."
Arjun looked at the bowl again. Brinjal on top. Potato at the bottom. A lotus slice with holes. "Every vegetable is a part of a plant," he said. "And each part is different inside."
"Then let's find out which part each one is," said Kavya. And they went to look in the vegetable basket.
story.epiphany: Whether a plant part floats or sinks does not depend on its size. It depends on what is inside it: stored food, or tiny spaces full of air.
ask: Why did Arjun think the potato sank?
How did Kavya test his idea?
Why does a lotus stem have holes?
What did Kavya say a cactus's spines are?
art: A girl and her grandmother at a kitchen sink in Madurai, a steel bowl of water with brinjal pieces floating and potato pieces at the bottom, and a small boy on a stool watching.
A grandmother holding a slice of lotus stem up to a window, the light shining through its ring of holes, with two children looking up at it.

experiments.title: The Float Test: which plant parts float, and which sink?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put pieces of six plant parts in a bowl of water: potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana. You guess first, then watch which float and which sink. Then you test if a tiny piece does anything different.
experiments.question: Which plant parts float in water, and which sink? Does a tiny piece do the same as a big piece?
experiments.predict: Hold each piece in your hand. Which ones will float, and which will sink? Put them in two groups. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece goes into the same bowl of the same tap water. We drop each piece in gently from just above the water, and wait 10 seconds before we decide. The four cut pieces (potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber) are all about the size of your thumb, so size is not the reason one floats and another sinks. The leaf and the chana go in as they are. Then we change only the size, with one tiny piece of potato and one tiny piece of brinjal.

materials.item: a big steel bowl, a vessel or a bucket, filled with tap water at least 10 cm deep
a potato
a carrot
a brinjal, any kind
a cucumber
a palak leaf, or a cabbage leaf, or any leaf vegetable
dry chana or dry rajma, straight from the packet
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a spoon, to fish the pieces out
a towel, for spills

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting.

schedule.what: Guess. Drop in six plant parts. Test a tiny piece of potato and of brinjal. Look inside a cut brinjal and potato. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Draw the bowl. Draw each food at the top of the water or at the bottom, where it really went. Write F for float or S for sink next to your guess.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting thumb-sized pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal and cucumber on a board, next to a palak leaf and five dry chana.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts thumb-sized pieces.

setup.art: A child holding a piece of potato in one hand and a piece of brinjal in the other, as if weighing them.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each piece. Guess: float or sink?

setup.art: A steel bowl of water with brinjal, cucumber and a palak leaf floating, and potato, carrot and chana on the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Drop each piece in gently. Wait 10 seconds.

setup.art: A tiny crumb of potato sinking in the water, and a tiny piece of brinjal floating beside a big piece.
setup.caption: 4. Try a tiny piece of potato and of brinjal.

setup.art: A brinjal piece and a potato piece cut open side by side, the brinjal spongy and the potato firm and white.
setup.caption: 5. Look inside a cut brinjal and a cut potato.

flow.do: 1. Cut one thumb-sized piece each of potato, carrot, brinjal and cucumber. 2. Lay them on a plate with a palak leaf and 5 dry chana. 3. Fill the bowl with water.
flow.say: Here are six foods. Each one is a part of a plant. Can you tell me which part each one is?
flow.kid: Look at the six foods. Each one is a part of a plant. Which part is each one?

ask.q: Which part of the plant is the carrot? And the chana?
good: The carrot is a root. It grew in the soil.
The chana is a seed. It can grow into a new plant.

flow.parent: Accept any answer now. The vegetable basket sort and the card game explain the parts. Potato is a stem that grows under the ground, which surprises most people.

flow.do: 1. Let your child hold each piece. 2. Ask them to put the pieces in two groups: will float, will sink. 3. Write down their groups and their reason, word for word.
flow.say: Hold each piece in your hand. Which ones will float, and which will sink? Make two groups. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hold each piece. Will it float or sink? Make two groups. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put that one in the sink group?
good: It feels heavy.
It is hard.
Seeds are small, so I think they float.

flow.parent: Most children say heavy or hard things sink. Do not say if they are right. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Your child drops each piece in gently, one at a time, from just above the water. 2. Count to 10 together after each one. 3. Your child says float or sink, and you write it in the table.
flow.say: Drop the first piece in gently. Let's count to ten. Is it on top, or at the bottom?
flow.kid: Drop one piece in gently. Count to ten. Is it on top or at the bottom?
flow.parent: Usually the brinjal, cucumber and palak leaf float. The potato and dry chana sink. Most carrots sink, but a few float. Write down what yours really did. If a piece floats with a bubble stuck to it, push it under once and let go.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up breaks off a crumb of potato, as small as a grain of rice. 2. Cut a tiny piece of brinjal the same size. 3. Ask your child to guess first. 4. Drop both in.
flow.say: Some people say small things float and big things sink. Here is a tiny bit of potato. Will it float or sink? Why?
flow.kid: Here is a tiny bit of potato. Will it float or sink? Say why. Now drop it in.

ask.q: The tiny potato sank, and the big brinjal floated. So is it about size?
good: No. The tiny potato still sank.
It is what is inside that decides.

check.q: A tiny crumb of potato sank. A big piece of brinjal floated. What does this show?
options: Size is not what matters. What is inside matters.
Potato only sinks in cold water
check.why: If size decided, the tiny crumb would float and the big brinjal would sink. The opposite happened. So what is inside the part decides.

flow.do: 1. Cut a brinjal piece and a potato piece in half. 2. Let your child look closely and press each one with a finger. 3. Ask what is different inside.
flow.say: Look inside the brinjal and the potato. Press each one. What is different?
flow.kid: Look inside the brinjal and the potato. Press each one. What is different?

ask.q: What is the brinjal like inside?
good: Soft and spongy.
It has tiny holes.
It squashes.

ask.q: What is the potato like inside?
good: Hard and firm.
Packed tight.
No holes.

flow.parent: Now explain. A brinjal is spongy, with tiny spaces full of air, so it floats. A leaf has air spaces too, because a leaf takes in air to make food. A potato, a carrot and a seed are packed with food the plant stored for later, so they sink.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they found in three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why. 2. Write it at the bottom of the table.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. Which parts floated? Which parts sank? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Which floated? Which sank? Why?

ask.q: Why did the potato and the chana sink?
good: They are packed with stored food.
There is no air inside them.

experiments.title: Do Seeds Drink? Ten chana in water overnight
experiments.context: In this experiment you line up 10 dry chana along a ruler, then soak them in water overnight. The next morning you line them up again and see how much longer the line has become.
experiments.question: Does a dry seed take in water? How much bigger does a line of 10 chana get after a night in water?
experiments.predict: Look at the dry chana. After a night in water, will the line of 10 chana be shorter, the same, or longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same 10 chana before and after. We line them up the same way each time, touching end to end along the ruler. We keep 10 more dry chana in a dry cup, so we can compare.
results_table: Length of the line after one night (cm)

materials.item: dry kabuli chana or kala chana, straight from the packet
two small steel bowls or cups
a ruler with centimetres
water

schedule.what: Line up 10 dry chana along the ruler and measure. Put them in water. Put 10 more chana in a dry cup.
Line up the 10 soaked chana again and measure. Compare them with the dry ones. Press one of each.

experiments.record: Draw a dry chana and a soaked chana side by side, the real size. Write the length of the line before and after.

setup.art: Ten dry chana in a straight line touching end to end along a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Line up 10 dry chana. Measure the line.

setup.art: Ten chana in a steel bowl of water, and ten more in a dry steel bowl beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Soak 10. Keep 10 dry.

setup.art: Ten plump soaked chana in a longer line along the ruler, next to a line of ten small dry ones.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, measure the soaked line again.

flow.do: 1. Your child lines up 10 dry chana touching end to end along the ruler. 2. Read the length together and write it down. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Here is a line of 10 dry chana. Tomorrow, after a night in water, will the line be shorter, the same, or longer? Why?
flow.kid: Line up 10 chana on the ruler. How long is the line? Will it change after a night in water? Why?

good: Longer, because the seeds drink the water.
The same, because seeds are hard.

flow.do: 1. Put the 10 measured chana in a bowl and cover them with water. 2. Put 10 more dry chana in the other cup, with no water. 3. Leave both overnight.
flow.say: Let's soak these ten. These other ten stay dry, so tomorrow we can compare.
flow.kid: Put 10 chana in water. Put 10 more in a dry cup. Leave them for the night.

flow.do: 1. Drain the soaked chana. 2. Your child lines them up along the ruler again. 3. Read the length and write it down. 4. Press a dry chana and a soaked one between finger and thumb.
flow.say: Line up the soaked chana. How long is the line now? Press a soaked one and a dry one. What is different?
flow.kid: Line up the soaked chana. How long is the line now? Press one. Is it soft?

ask.q: Where did the extra size come from?
good: The chana drank water.
Water went inside the seed.

flow.parent: Soaked chana are usually a little bigger and softer: the line of 10 often grows by 1 to 3 centimetres, and a soaked chana dents when you press it. Write down what yours really did. A seed is packed with stored food, and the seed takes in water before the baby plant inside starts to grow. This is why we soak chana before cooking.

activities.title: The Vegetable Basket Sort: which part are we eating?
activities.context: In this activity you take the vegetables and dal from your kitchen and sort them onto six papers: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed. Then you cut open one to check a rule: if it has seeds inside, it is a fruit.

materials.item: six sheets of paper, and a pen to write on them
whatever vegetables, fruits and dals are in your kitchen today, for example carrot, onion, potato, palak, coriander, tomato, brinjal, bhindi, cauliflower, toor dal and rice
a tomato or a brinjal, and a knife for the grown-up

schedule.what: Lay out six papers. Sort the kitchen foods by plant part. Cut a tomato to check for seeds.

activities.record: Draw one food on each paper, and write its name.

setup.art: Six labelled sheets on the kitchen floor: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out six papers.

setup.art: A child putting a carrot on the root paper and a bunch of coriander on the leaf paper, with a basket of vegetables beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Put each food on the paper for its part.

setup.art: A tomato cut in half on a board, showing its seeds, with a child pointing at them.
setup.caption: 3. Cut a tomato. Seeds inside means fruit.

flow.do: 1. Write root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed, one on each of six sheets of paper. 2. Lay them out and read each label with your child. 3. Bring the vegetable basket and the dal tins.
flow.say: Every plant food is one part of a plant. Let's find out which part each of our foods is.
flow.kid: Look at the six papers. Root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed. Bring the vegetables.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks up one food at a time. 2. They say which part they think it is and why. 3. They put it on that paper. 4. Help only with the surprises.
flow.say: Pick up a food. Which plant part do you think this food is? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Pick up a food. Which part is it? Put it on that paper.

ask.q: How did you know the carrot is a root?
good: It grows in the soil.
It is long and pointed, with thin hairs.

flow.parent: Surprises: a potato is a stem that grows under the ground. An onion is mostly fat leaves wrapped round each other. Cauliflower is a bunch of tiny flower buds. Tomato, brinjal, bhindi and cucumber are fruits.

flow.do: 1. Cut a tomato or a brinjal in half. 2. Ask your child what they see inside. 3. Ask which paper it belongs on.
flow.say: Here is a rule scientists use. If it grew from a flower and has seeds inside, it is a fruit. Look inside this tomato. Which paper does it go on?
flow.kid: Look inside the tomato. Can you see seeds? Seeds inside means it is a fruit.

check.q: You cut a bhindi and find a row of seeds inside. Which part of the plant is a bhindi?
check.why: A part that grew from a flower and holds seeds is a fruit. A cook calls bhindi a vegetable, but a scientist calls it a fruit.

activities.title: The Masala Box Hunt: plant parts in your spices
activities.context: In this activity you open the masala box and find out which plant part each spice comes from. Many spices are parts you would never guess.

materials.item: the masala box from your kitchen, or the spice jars you have
a steel plate
the six plant part papers from the vegetable basket sort

schedule.what: Open the masala box. Put a pinch of each spice on the right plant part paper.

activities.record: Draw each spice you found on its paper, and write its name.

setup.art: An open round steel masala box with turmeric, mustard seeds, methi seeds, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies in its little cups.
setup.caption: 1. Open the masala box.

setup.art: A clove held close up between two fingers, showing its round tiny bud at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely at each spice. Which part is it?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the six plant part papers, or write the six names on new papers. 2. Open the masala box and let your child smell each spice. 3. Put a pinch of each on a steel plate.
flow.say: Every spice in this box came from a plant. Smell each one. Which plant part do you think each spice is?
flow.kid: Smell each spice. Every one came from a plant. Which part do you think?

flow.do: 1. Tell your child each answer after they have guessed. 2. They move the pinch to the right paper.
flow.say: Guess first, then I will tell you. Which part of a plant do you think this spice is?
flow.kid: Guess first. Then put each spice on its paper.

good: The clove, because it is a flower.
Cinnamon, because it is the bark of a stem.

flow.parent: Answers: mustard and methi are seeds. Dried red chilli is a fruit with seeds inside. Turmeric is an underground stem. Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree's stem. A clove is a flower bud that was picked and dried before it opened. Leave out jeera: it is a tiny fruit that looks like a seed. A powder such as turmeric or chilli powder cannot be recognised, so use the whole spice if you have it, or tell your child which one it is.

activities.title: Three Plants, Three Homes: a cactus, a lotus and a banyan
activities.context: In this activity you draw a cactus, a lotus and a banyan side by side, and compare their roots, stems and leaves. Then you act out each plant with your body.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or three notebook pages
pencil and crayons
a cactus or a succulent in a pot, if you have one

schedule.what: Draw three plants. Mark their roots, stems and leaves. Act out each one.

activities.record: Draw the three plants side by side. Under each, write where the plant lives.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into three columns, with a cactus, a lotus and a banyan being drawn by a child.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the three plants side by side.

setup.art: A child standing still with arms tight at her sides like a cactus, another lying with arms spread like a lotus leaf, and another with arms out and dangling fingers like banyan roots.
setup.caption: 2. Act out each plant.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child what each plant looks like, using the notes below. 2. Your child draws all three. 3. They colour the roots brown, the stems orange and the leaves green. These colours are a code to tell the parts apart, not the real colours.
flow.say: Draw a cactus, a lotus and a banyan. Colour the roots brown, the stems orange and the leaves green. Where are the leaves on the cactus?
flow.kid: Draw the three plants. Roots brown, stems orange, leaves green.

ask.q: Why is the cactus stem so fat?
good: It keeps water inside.
It lives where it hardly rains.

ask.q: Where does the lotus stem grow?
good: In the mud at the bottom of the pond.

flow.parent: Cactus: a fat green stem full of water, sharp spines instead of flat leaves, and roots that spread wide just under the sand. Lotus: a stem lying in the mud at the bottom of a pond, long leaf stalks rising from it, and big round leaves on the water. Banyan: a huge tree with roots hanging down from her branches. The cactus's spines are their leaves, so colour them green too.

flow.do: 1. Call out a plant. 2. Your child acts it out and says one thing about its parts. 3. Swap, and let your child call out.
flow.say: Be a cactus! Now be a lotus! Now be a banyan! Tell me one thing about your roots or your stem.
flow.kid: Be a cactus. Be a lotus. Be a banyan. Say one thing about your roots or stem.
flow.parent: Cactus: stand tall and keep still, holding water in. Lotus: lie flat with arms spread like leaves on the water. Banyan: arms out wide, fingers hanging down like roots reaching for the ground.

activities.title: Count the Holes in a Lotus Stem (if you can buy one)
activities.context: Lotus stem is sold in many markets: thamarai thandu in Tamil Nadu, kamal kakdi in much of North India, nadru in Kashmir and bhein in Sindhi homes. In this activity you cut a slice, count the holes, and test if it floats.

materials.item: one lotus stem, from a vegetable market or a big shop. If you cannot find one, read the lotus stem part of the story again and draw the ring of holes it describes
a knife and a board, for the grown-up
a bowl of water

schedule.what: Cut slices of lotus stem. Count the holes. Hold a slice to the light. Test if a slice floats.

activities.record: Draw your slice, real size, with every hole.

setup.art: A pale lotus stem on a board, with one round slice cut off showing a ring of holes.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a thin slice.

setup.art: A child holding a lotus stem slice up to a window, with light shining through the holes.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it to the light. Count the holes.

flow.do: 1. Wash the lotus stem. 2. Cut two thin slices. 3. Your child holds one up to the light and counts the holes.
flow.say: This stem grew in the mud at the bottom of a pond. Look through it. How many holes can you count?
flow.kid: Hold the slice up to the light. Count the holes. Big ones and small ones.

ask.q: What do you think goes through these holes?
good: Air.
Air going down to the mud.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess if a slice will float or sink, and why. 2. Drop a slice into the bowl. 3. Talk about what happened.
flow.say: Will this slice float or sink? Why do you think so? Let's try.
flow.kid: Will the slice float or sink? Say why. Drop it in.
flow.parent: The holes are air tunnels. They carry air from the leaves above the water down to the stem in the mud. A cut slice is open at both ends, so water can fill the holes, and a lotus stem also stores food. So nobody can promise what your slice will do: write down what it really did, and ask your child why.

games.title: Which Part Do We Eat?
games.context: This is a card game about the plant parts we eat. You turn over a food card, say which plant part the food is, and check the back.

items.b: Stem. A potato is a stem that grows under the ground.
Leaf. A cabbage is many leaves wrapped tight.
Flower. It is a bunch of tiny flower buds.
Flower. A clove is a dried flower bud.
Fruit. It grew from a flower and has seeds inside.
Fruit. The long pod holds the seeds.

printables.title: 6 part cards to cut out: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed

rules: Lay the 6 part cards face up in a row. Mix the 18 food cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. On your turn, turn over the top food card and read the food aloud.
Put the food card under the part you think it is, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card in your own pile. If not, leave the card under its right part, and nobody keeps it.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most kept cards wins. If two players tie, they share the win. Then put every card under its part and count how many cards each part has.

setup.art: Six part cards in a row on a table, root to seed, with a face-down pile of food cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 6 part cards. Pile up the food cards.

setup.art: A child placing a tomato card under the fruit card while her brother watches.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a food. Put it under its part. Check the back.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Lay out the 6 part cards. 3. A child who cannot read yet can first draw a small picture of the food on each food card.
flow.say: Let's cut out the cards. Then we can play.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay out the 6 part cards. You can draw each food on its card.

flow.do: 1. Take turns as the rules say. 2. On each turn, ask the player why they chose that part.
flow.say: Turn over a card. Which part is it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Which part is it? Say why. Check the back.

check.q: Which of these is a flower that we eat?
check.why: A cauliflower is a bunch of tiny flower buds. A carrot is a root and rice is a seed.

flow.do: 1. Lay out all the cards under their parts. 2. Count each group together.
flow.say: Which part of the plant do we eat the most of? Let's count.
flow.kid: Count the cards under each part. Which has the most?

games.title: Cactus, Lotus or Banyan?
games.context: This is a clue game. One player reads a clue about a plant's roots, stem or leaves. The others guess: cactus, lotus or banyan?

items.f: My stem is fat and green, and full of water.
I live where it hardly rains for months.
My roots spread wide just under the sand, to catch rain fast.
My stem lies in the mud at the bottom of a pond.
My leaf stalks are full of air tunnels.
My big round leaves rest on the water or stand just above it.
Water rolls off my leaves in round drops.
My roots hang down from my branches like ropes.
When my hanging roots reach the soil, they grow thick like pillars.
Birds eat my small red figs and drop my seeds far away.
One of me can spread so wide that I look like a whole forest.

printables.title: 12 answer cards: cactus, lotus and banyan for up to 4 players

rules: Each player takes one cactus, one lotus and one banyan answer card.
Mix the clue cards and put them face down. One player is the reader.
The reader turns over a clue card and reads the front aloud, but not the back. The reader does not answer that round.
Everyone else holds up the answer card they think is right, all at the same time.
The reader reads the back. Everyone who was right gets one point.
The next player becomes the reader. Play until all 12 clues are read. The player with the most points wins. If two players tie, they share the win.

setup.art: Three hand-drawn answer cards, a cactus, a lotus and a banyan, in front of each of three players.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes three answer cards.

setup.art: A girl reading a clue card aloud while two others hold up their banyan cards.
setup.caption: 2. Read a clue. Everyone holds up an answer.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the clue cards and the answer cards. 2. Give each player a cactus, a lotus and a banyan answer card. 3. Mix the clue cards.
flow.say: Here are your three answer cards. You will hold one up when you hear a clue.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Take a cactus, a lotus and a banyan answer card.

flow.do: 1. Play as the rules say. 2. After each clue, ask why that part helps the plant.
flow.say: Listen to the clue. Hold up your answer. Why does that part help the plant?
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Hold up cactus, lotus or banyan.

check.q: Which plant keeps air tunnels in their stalks?
check.why: A lotus grows their stem in pond mud, where there is almost no air. Air tunnels carry air down from the leaves.

projects.title: Roots from a Stem: a money plant or mint in a jar
projects.context: A banyan grows roots from her branches. Many plants can grow roots from their stems. In this two-week project you put a piece of money plant or mint stem in a jar of water and watch new roots grow out of the stem.

materials.item: a piece of money plant stem with 3 or 4 leaves and at least one bump where a leaf was joined, cut by a grown-up, or 2 stems from a bunch of pudina (mint) from the market
a clear glass jar or a clear plastic bottle with the top cut off
tap water

schedule.what: Pull the bottom leaves off the stem. Put the stem in a jar of water on a bright windowsill, out of strong sun.
Look for tiny white bumps or roots on the stem under the water. Top up the water.
Count the roots. Draw the stem and roots. Change the water.
Count the roots again. Draw them. Say where on the stem they grew.

projects.record: Draw the stem on day 1, day 9 and day 14. Write how many roots you can count each time.

setup.art: A money plant stem with the bottom leaves pulled off, standing in a clear jar of water on a windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Put a stem in a jar of water.

setup.art: The same jar a week later, with thin white roots growing from bumps on the stem under the water.
setup.caption: 2. Watch roots grow out of the stem.

flow.do: 1. Cut a piece of money plant stem with 3 or 4 leaves, or use two mint stems. 2. Your child pulls off the lowest leaves. 3. Put the stem in a jar of water. 4. Keep the bare part under the water, with one leaf bump. 5. Your child draws the stem.
flow.say: Roots usually grow from a seed, down into the soil. Can roots grow out of a stem? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Pull off the bottom leaves. Put the stem in the water. Will roots grow?

ask.q: Do you think roots will grow? Where on the stem?
good: Yes, at the bottom.
Where the leaves were.

flow.parent: Mint usually grows roots within about a week. Money plant often takes one to three weeks. Roots usually grow from the bumps on the stem where leaves were joined.

flow.do: 1. Look at the stem under the water together. 2. Top up the water.
flow.say: Can you see any white bumps or roots yet? Where are they growing from?
flow.kid: Look under the water. Can you see white bumps or roots?

flow.do: 1. Count the roots together. 2. Your child draws the stem and roots. 3. Change the water.
flow.say: How many roots can you count? Draw them.
flow.kid: Count the roots. Draw them.

flow.do: 1. Count the roots again. 2. Your child draws the final picture. 3. Talk about the banyan.
flow.say: These roots grew out of a stem, not from a seed. A banyan does the same, high up in the air. Where did your roots grow from?
flow.kid: Count the roots. Where did they grow from? A banyan grows roots from branches too.

ask.q: How is your stem like a banyan branch?
good: Roots grew out of the stem.
Both grow roots from a stem, not from a seed.

flow.parent: You can plant the rooted stem in a pot of soil to keep it growing.

projects.safety: Money plant sap can upset the stomach and the mouth. Do not chew it, keep it from small children and pets, and wash hands after cutting it. A grown-up cuts the stem, and the bottle if you use one.

challenges.title: Hold Up a Long Branch, the Banyan Way
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. You make a paper tree with one long branch. The branch droops. Then you hold it up with prop roots, the way a banyan holds up her long branches.
challenges.problem: Make a paper branch at least 40 cm long, sticking out sideways from a steel tumbler trunk. Hang a clothes peg on the end. The branch must not touch the table.
constraints: Use only newspaper, sticky tape, a steel tumbler and a clothes peg.
The branch must stick out sideways, not upwards.
Use at most 8 pieces of sticky tape.
materials: a steel tumbler, upside down, as the trunk
a ruler or a measuring tape
general: Roll the newspaper very tight, so the branch is stiffer.
Add rolled newspaper prop roots from the branch straight down to the table, like a banyan.
creative: Make the branch from two rolls taped side by side, so it is thicker.
Add many thin prop roots instead of one thick one, and see which holds better.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own branch. How long can you make it before it touches the table? Count how many prop roots you needed.

setup.art: An upside-down steel tumbler with a long rolled newspaper branch taped to it, drooping down to the table with a clothes peg on the end.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a long paper branch to the tumbler. It droops.

setup.art: The same branch held up straight by two rolled newspaper pillars going down from the branch to the table, like banyan roots.
setup.caption: 2. Add prop roots under the branch.

flow.do: 1. Roll two sheets of newspaper into a long, tight tube. 2. Tape it to the upside-down tumbler so it sticks out sideways. 3. Hang the clothes peg on the end.
flow.say: Here is our tree with one long branch. Hang the peg on the end. What happens?
flow.kid: Roll a long paper branch. Tape it to the tumbler. Hang the peg. What happens?

good: It is too long and heavy at the end.
Nothing holds it up.

flow.parent: A tight newspaper roll may hold one peg at first. If it does not droop, make the branch longer, or hang a second peg, until it does.

flow.do: 1. Roll thinner tubes for prop roots. 2. Your child tapes them from the branch straight down to the table. 3. Hang the peg again.
flow.say: A banyan grows roots down from her branches. When they reach the ground, they hold the branch up. Can you make prop roots for your branch?
flow.kid: Roll thin paper roots. Tape them from the branch down to the table. Hang the peg again.

check.q: How does a banyan hold up a very long branch?
options: The branch is made of stone
Roots grow down from the branch and act like pillars
check.why: Prop roots grow down from the branch into the soil and get thick. They hold the branch up, so the tree can spread very wide.

flow.do: 1. Measure how long the branch is now. 2. Count the prop roots. 3. Ask your child how they would make it even longer.
flow.say: How long is your branch now? How many prop roots did it need? How could a banyan spread even wider?
flow.kid: Measure your branch. Count the roots. How could it grow longer?

items.p: Draw a line from each food to its plant part.
items.why: A carrot grows down in the soil like a root. Sugarcane is a tall stem. Palak is a leaf. Cauliflower is a bunch of flower buds. A tomato has seeds inside, so it is a fruit. Rice is a seed.

items.p: In the float test, what happened to the piece of potato?
items.why: A potato is packed with stored food, with little room for air, so it sinks.
items.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.

items.p: Sort these by what they did in the float test.
items.why: The parts with air spaces floated. The parts packed with stored food sank.
items.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.

items.p: Draw the bowl of water from your float test. Draw each food where it really went: at the top or at the bottom.
items.a: A bowl with brinjal, cucumber and the leaf at the top, and potato and chana at the bottom
items.why: A strong drawing puts each food where it really went in the child's own test, even if a piece did something unusual.
items.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.

items.p: Three of these are leaves we eat. Which one is not a leaf?
items.why: A carrot is a root. Palak, curry leaves and cabbage are all leaves.

items.p: Label the parts of the cactus: stem, spines, roots.
a: the parts under the sand: roots
items.why: A cactus has a fat stem that stores water, spines that are changed leaves, and roots that spread under the sand.
items.art: A drawing of a cactus in sand, with three empty label lines pointing to the stem, the spines and the roots.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 2, sorts her vegetable basket. She finds 3 roots, 2 leaves and 4 fruits. How many foods did she sort?
items.context: This question is about the vegetable basket sort. You sort the vegetables at home by which part of the plant each one is.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the tiny crumb of potato sink?
items.a: Because the potato is packed with stored food inside. Size does not change what is inside
items.why: A strong answer says that what is inside decides, not the size of the piece.
items.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.

items.p: The sharp points on a cactus are changed ____.
items.why: Cactus spines grow where leaves grow on other plants. They lose much less water than flat leaves.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, and her cousin Arjun, aged 6, are looking at a tomato.

views.says: A tomato is a fruit. It grew from a flower and has seeds inside.
A tomato is a vegetable. We put it in sambar, not in sweets.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side with a reason, then says the other is also right in its own way
items.why: Both are right in their own place. A scientist names a part by how it grew. A cook names a food by how it is used.

items.p: Draw a line from each plant to where they live.
pairs: a dry place where it hardly rains
open ground with room to spread
items.why: Each plant's parts suit their home: water stored in a cactus stem, air tunnels in a lotus stalk, prop roots for a banyan's wide branches.

items.p: Why does a lotus stem have holes in it?
opts: They are tunnels that carry air down to the stem in the mud
To make the stem lighter to cook
items.why: Mud at the bottom of a pond has almost no air. The tunnels carry air from the leaves down to the stem.

items.p: Draw a banyan tree with three prop roots. Draw an arrow on one root to show which way it grew.
items.a: A banyan with roots hanging down from the branches and arrows pointing down to the soil
items.why: A strong drawing shows the roots growing down from the branches, not up from the ground.

items.p: Almost all cactus plants first grew in North and South America.
items.why: True. People brought prickly pear cactus to India long ago, and now it grows wild in dry places.

items.p: A leaf floated in the float test. Say or write one reason why.
items.a: A leaf has tiny air spaces inside, because a leaf takes in air to make food
items.why: A strong answer names the air spaces, and says the leaf uses air.
items.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.

items.p: A banyan's prop roots grow down from the ____ to the soil.
items.why: Prop roots start high up on the branches and grow down. When they reach the soil, they get thick and hold the branch up.

items.p: Sort these parts into the plant they belong to.
items.why: Each plant has the same kinds of parts, shaped for a different home.

items.p: Label the lotus: leaf, leaf stalk, stem in the mud, roots.
a: the round part on the water: leaf
the long part going down: leaf stalk
the long part lying in the mud: stem
the thin parts in the mud: roots
items.why: The lotus stem lies in the mud. Long stalks rise from it to the leaves on the water.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of a pond with a lotus, and four empty label lines.

items.p: Three of these are fruits. Which one is not a fruit?
items.why: Sugarcane is a stem. Brinjal, bhindi and drumstick all grew from flowers and hold seeds, so they are fruits.

items.p: Three people talk about a cactus.

views.says: Spines are best. They lose almost no water, and animals do not eat the plant.
Flat leaves are best. They catch lots of light and make lots of food.
It depends on where the plant lives.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that spines suit a dry place and flat leaves suit a wet one
items.why: Each part has a cost and a gain. Spines save water but make little food. Flat leaves make more food but lose more water.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Class 2, drops a dry chana into water and it sinks. She soaks another chana overnight, then drops it in. What do you think happens?
opts: The soaked chana floats because it took in water
items.why: Soaking fills the seed with water, but the seed is still packed with stored food, so the chana still sinks. Water inside does not make a part float. Air spaces do.
items.context: This question joins the float test and the seed soak. You tested which parts float and measured chana before and after a night in water.

items.p: A clove is a dried flower bud. Say or write why we cannot see that it is a flower.
items.a: It was picked before it opened, and it was dried, so it is small, brown and hard
items.why: A strong answer says the bud was picked before it opened, and drying changed how it looks.

items.p: Invent a plant that lives in a pond in a desert. Draw their roots, stem and leaves. Show one part that keeps water and one that brings air down.
items.a: Any plant that has, for example, a fat stem for water and hollow stalks for air
items.why: A strong drawing gives each part a clear job and explains it in a label.

items.p: Put the steps of the seed soak in order.
items: Line up 10 dry chana and measure.
Line them up again and measure.
items.why: Measure first, then soak, then measure again, then compare. Without the first measurement, we cannot tell how much the seeds grew.
items.context: This question is about the seed soak. You measure a line of 10 dry chana, soak them overnight, and measure again.

items.p: In the seed soak, the line of soaked chana was ____ than the line of dry chana.
items.why: The seeds took in water and swelled.
items.context: This question is about the seed soak. You measure a line of 10 dry chana, soak them overnight, and measure again.

items.p: The roots of the money plant in the jar grew out of a seed.
items.why: False. They grew out of the stem, usually where a leaf had been joined. A banyan grows roots from her branches in the same way.
items.context: This question is about the jar project. You put a money plant or mint stem in a jar of water and watch roots grow.

items.p: Label each food with its plant part: turmeric, mustard seeds, cinnamon, dried red chilli.
items.why: Turmeric is an underground stem. Cinnamon is the bark of a stem. Mustard seeds are seeds. A chilli grew from a flower and holds seeds, so it is a fruit.
items.art: Four small pictures of spices with an empty label under each.
items.context: This question is about the masala box hunt, where you found which plant part each spice comes from.

items.p: A lotus stem slice has holes. Bijoya, a girl in Kolkata, drops a slice in water. Say or write what you think will happen, and why.
items.a: Any guess with a reason. For example: it may float because of the air in the holes, or sink because the stem also stores food
items.why: A strong answer gives a guess and a reason that uses what the child knows about air spaces and stored food. Testing is the only way to be sure.

items.p: Why do farmers sometimes put seeds in water before they sow them, and throw away the ones that float?
opts: Floating seeds are often empty or damaged inside
Water makes seeds grow faster in a minute
items.why: A good seed is packed with stored food, so the seed sinks. A seed that floats often has air where their food should be.

items.p: Two people talk about the banyan.

views.says: The banyan's prop roots are roots. They grow down and drink water from the soil.
Once they get thick and hold the branch up, they are really trunks.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that prop roots start as roots and take on the job of a trunk
items.why: Prop roots begin as roots and take in water from the soil. Later they also hold the tree up, like a trunk. A part can do more than one job.

videos.title: A banyan tree's hanging roots growing down to the ground
videos.why: Shows prop roots growing from branches and turning into pillars.
videos.check: Find a real video, check that it shows a banyan (Ficus benghalensis), and watch it fully first.

videos.title: A lotus pond: leaves, stalks and the stem in the mud
videos.why: Shows where each lotus part grows, and the holes in a cut lotus stem.
videos.check: Find a real video and watch it first.

quiz.p: Which part of the plant is a carrot?
quiz.why: A carrot grows down in the soil and stores food. It is a root. Picking 'fruit' may mean thinking every orange food is a fruit.

quiz.p: Which of these is a seed?
quiz.why: Dal is a seed. Palak is a leaf and sugarcane is a stem.

quiz.p: Hema, a girl in Class 2, drops a piece of brinjal into water. What happens?
quiz.why: A brinjal is spongy, with tiny air spaces, so it floats.

quiz.p: Why do potato pieces and dry chana sink?
opts: They are packed with stored food
quiz.why: Stored food is packed tight, with little room for air. Picking 'full of air' mixes them up with the floaters.

quiz.p: An onion is made of layers wrapped round each other. Which plant part are most of those layers?
quiz.why: Most of an onion is fat leaves wrapped round each other. Picking roots may mean thinking anything that grows low down is a root.

quiz.p: Where does a lotus keep their stem?
opts: In the mud at the bottom of the pond
quiz.why: The lotus stem lies in the mud. Air tunnels bring air down to it.

quiz.p: How do a banyan's prop roots help the tree?
opts: They hold up the long branches like pillars
quiz.why: Prop roots grow down from the branches into the soil, then get thick and hold the branches up.

quiz.p: Why does a cactus have a fat stem?
opts: To store water for dry months
quiz.why: A cactus lives where it hardly rains, so their stem stores water. Floating is the lotus, and pillars are the banyan.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, says a tomato is a fruit. Why is he right?
opts: It grew from a flower and has seeds inside
quiz.why: A fruit grows from a flower and holds seeds. Colour and taste are not what make a fruit.

quiz.p: Ila, a girl in Class 2, wants to find out if a piece of cucumber floats. What should she do first?
opts: Look it up and skip the test
quiz.why: A scientist guesses first and gives a reason, then tests to see what really happens.

applications: Cooks soak dal and chana before cooking, because dry seeds take in water and get soft.
Gardeners grow new money plants, tulsi and mint by putting cut stems in water until roots grow.
Lotus stem is cooked in many parts of India: thamarai thandu in Tamil Nadu, kamal kakdi in much of North India, nadru in Kashmir.
Makhana, the puffed snack from Bihar, is the seed of the fox-nut plant, a kind of water lily that grows in ponds.

open_questions.q: How does a banyan's hanging root know which way is down, and when it has reached the soil?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know roots sense gravity with tiny heavy grains in their tips. How a hanging root then changes into a thick pillar once it touches the ground is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a lotus push air down to the stem in the mud?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that warm leaves push air down the stalks. Just how much each part of the leaf does, and how the flow changes from day to night, is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the float test, 3 foods floated and 3 foods sank. How many foods did you test?
maths.context: This question is about the float test. You put pieces of potato, carrot, brinjal, cucumber, a palak leaf and dry chana in a bowl of water, and see which float and which sink.
maths.why_maths: Adding the two groups checks that we tested every food and did not lose one.

maths.problem: A line of 10 dry chana was 9 cm long. After a night in water, the line was 12 cm long. How much longer did it get?
maths.explain: Count on from 9 to 12: 10, 11, 12. That is 3 steps, so the line got 3 cm longer.
maths.context: This question is about the seed soak. You measure a line of 10 dry chana, soak them overnight, and measure again.
maths.why_maths: Taking the 'before' length from the 'after' length tells us how much water made the seeds grow.

maths.problem: Kavya sorted her vegetable basket and made a tally: roots ||, stems |, leaves ||||, fruits |||. Which part did she have the most of? How many more leaves than fruits?
maths.explain: Leaves have 4 marks, the most. Fruits have 3. 4 take away 3 is 1.
maths.context: This question is about the vegetable basket sort. You sort the vegetables at home by which part of the plant each one is.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which plant part we eat most of.

maths.problem: Your money plant grew 2 roots by day 5, and 2 more roots every 4 days after that. How many roots would it have on day 13?
maths.explain: Day 5: 2 roots. Day 9: 2 + 2 = 4 roots. Day 13: 4 + 2 = 6 roots. This is a made-up pattern. A real plant may grow faster or slower.
maths.context: This question is about the jar project. You put a money plant or mint stem in a jar of water and watch roots grow.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern lets us guess what comes next, and then the real plant shows if the guess was right.

roots.context: We have sorted our food by plant part, tested which parts float, and met a cactus, a lotus and a banyan. Now we ask what the float test tells us about plants, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Our potato piece and dry chana sank in the bowl. They are packed with food the plant stored for later. The palak leaf floated, because it is full of tiny air spaces. A leaf takes in air to make food, so each part is filled for its job.
deep_truth.habit: We think of vegetables as food that is the same all through, made for us. The float test showed that each part is filled differently inside: one with stored food, another with air. What fills a part tells us the job it was doing for the plant.
deep_truth.evidence: In the float test, the potato and dry chana sank, and a tiny crumb of potato sank too. The brinjal piece and the palak leaf floated. Cut open, the potato was firm and packed, and the brinjal was spongy. A lotus stem slice is full of air tunnels.

three.who_am_i: Your body is filled for its jobs too. Your lungs are full of tiny air spaces, and your bones are dense and strong.
three.what_is_life: A plant makes food and stores some for later, in a root, a stem or a seed. When we eat it, that saved food becomes ours.
three.what_is_this_world: A cactus, a lotus and a banyan all have roots, stems and leaves, but each is shaped by the place they live.

roots.thread: Most plants start as one seed. From that one seed come roots, a stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and new seeds, each filled and shaped for a different job. The same root, stem and leaf become a water store in a cactus, an air pipe in a lotus and a pillar in a banyan. Everything is conscious, the plant too: each part senses what is around that part and sends signals to the others, so the whole plant acts together.

teachings.teaching: A lotus stalk grows as long as the water is deep. In the same way, how high a person rises depends on how strong their will is.
teachings.link: A lotus grows their leaf stalks long enough to reach the top of the water. The Tirukkural, from Tamil Nadu, saw that a plant's part grows to fit the place.

teachings.teaching: A wise person acts in the world but is not stained by it, like a lotus leaf that sits on water and stays dry.
teachings.link: A lotus leaf rests on the water, and water rolls off in drops. The top of the leaf is waxy, so it stays dry.

science.text: Leaves have many tiny air spaces inside. Air moves through them to the cells that make the plant's food.
Whether plants feel what their parts are doing, the way we feel our hands, is still argued about.

other_view.view: They explain the parts of a plant without any mind. Over a very long time, plants with parts that suited their home lived and left more seeds. They do not use feeling or deciding to explain it.

practice.title: Feel the air inside you
practice.say: Sit still and put your hands on your chest. Breathe in slowly. Feel your chest get bigger as air fills the tiny spaces in your lungs. Breathe out slowly. A leaf has tiny air spaces too. Breathe in again, and think of a leaf taking in air in the sun.
practice.kid: Sit still. Put your hands on your chest. Breathe in slowly. Feel the air fill you. Breathe out. A leaf has air inside too.

ask: Your lungs have air spaces, and so does a leaf. What else in your body is filled for its job?
Is a banyan's prop root still a root once it holds the tree up?
roots.art: A child sitting still with hands on her chest, beside a large palak leaf floating on a bowl of water, with a lotus pond and a banyan in the background.

playtest: We walked through both card games with 2 and with 4 players, the float test, the chana soak, the kitchen sort, the masala box, the lotus slice, the jar of roots and the paper banyan, step by step as a family in a flat. We replaced banana stem (really a wrapped stack of leaf bases) with lotus stem on the card and in the examples, and added the missing step that writes the six plant-part papers for the sort and the masala box. We added the day-1 drawing the roots project promised and a note for when the paper branch does not droop, made the chana bowls agree, fixed double full stops in answers, replaced a quiz question that repeated a worksheet question, and took a doubtful blow-through-the-stalk memory out of the story.
